To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

family members can influence the diabetes self-care of older adults with T2DM through persuasion or pressure, but these forms of social control have complex and differential effects depending on patients’ levels of self-efficacy.

the use of family persuasion to influence self-care adherence in older adults with T2DM was not significantly associated with self-care adherence, while family pressure was significantly associated with self-efficacy.
Family members’ use of social control (pressure vs. persuasion) was associated with older adults’ diabetes self-care adherence and psychological functioning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of family members’ social control on the psychological functioning and diabetes self-care adherence of older adults with T2DM.
the role of family in the management of chronic disease in older adults.
understanding the relationship between family members’ social control and older adults’ diabetes management and psychological functioning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the study findings highlight the importance of the role that social control and self-efficacy play in the management of diabetes among older adults.

the use of social pressure by family members is not recommended, and that the use of persuasion by family members may be helpful for older adults with T2DM who have low self-efficacy for diabetes management.

persuasion was associated with less diabetes-related distress and depression, and pressure was associated with more diabetes-related distress and depressive symptoms, and that self-efficacy moderated the relationships between persuasion/pressure and emotional distress/depression.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

family members should use persuasive rather than pressure-based social control strategies, and that patients with low self-efficacy may benefit from family members’ use persuasion, whereas patients with higher self- efficacy may be adversely affected by persuasion.

family members’ use social pressure to encourage better self-care behaviors among older adults with T2DM may not always be beneficial, and may in fact have adverse effects on patients’ psychological functioning.
family members’ use social control in the form of persuasion and social pressure in their efforts to encourage better diabetes self-care among older adults.
The main takeaway from our work is that
family members’ use social control to influence patients’ adherence to self-care behaviors.

older adults who are more confident in their ability to manage their diabetes are more likely to be influenced in a positive way by family members who use persuasion to encourage them to take better care of themselves, whereas older adults who are less confident are more likely to experience emotional distress when family members use persuasion.

the family members’ use (or overuse) of pressure to encourage better diabetes self-management can have negative consequences on patients’ well-being, especially for patients with lower self-efficiency.
